item.title: Is Jordan Back in the Crosshairs of Terrorist Groups?
item.dc:creator: Nikkie Lyubarsky
item.description:

The post Is Jordan Back in the Crosshairs of Terrorist Groups? appeared first on The Soufan Center.
item.content:encoded:
In less than two weeks, Jordan has experienced two fatal terrorist attacks in its capital, Amman, and Karak governorate — marking the country’s first major terrorist incidents in a decade. The attacks have both sparked a race for the government to tighten security, increase punitive consequences for terrorists, and pursue accountability against the attackers, but have also raised important questions about whether Jordan is becoming a softer target for terrorist networks like Islamic State (IS).

In the village of Hamoud in Jordan’s Karak governorate, a funeral procession outside the St. George Greek Orthodox Church was attacked by three gunmen, who fired upon Christian worshippers in waves with one semi-automatic rifle and two handguns at the church’s entrance and courtyard. The attack resulted in nine individuals killed, along with at least 40 wounded. Jordanian security officers arrested the three gunmen — all Jordanian citizens and from the same family in Karak: Hazzah Zaidan Mohammad Thenibat, Mishal Zedian Mohammad Thenibat, and Ahmad Sami Hussein Thenibat — after armed clashes with them at an abandoned house in Karak’s Al Judaya village on October 26, where all three were wounded. The government reported that the gunmen were associated with IS and communicated with the group to identify several targets across Jordan.

While the Karak attack prompted the Jordanian government to swiftly adopt new changes to its counterterrorism infrastructure, with King Abdullah encouraging agencies to act with an “iron fist” and stepping up security at malls, public spaces, and embassies, a second attack followed less than two weeks later. Outside the Sri Lankan Embassy in Amman, an extremist stabbed a Public Security Directorate corporal and a security officer, killing one. Jordan’s Public Security Directorate deemed that the incident was a terrorist attack, though no terrorist group was explicitly named. In recent years, IS has refrained from directly claiming attacks, a strategy to blur lines of accountability and complicate intelligence efforts. Asharq Al-Awsat reported that the attacker was previously incarcerated in 2020 on terrorism charges, sentenced to nine years in prison in 2022, but was released early. The publication also stated that the attacker had pledged allegiance to the Islamic State in 2019.

The October 23 and November 5 attacks represented the first major terrorist incidents in roughly ten years. In the December 2016 attack, Karak was targeted by several IS militants who launched a raid against several sites in Jordan’s Karak, including a siege of a local castle. That attack killed at least ten people, with dozens more wounded. The fact that Karak was targeted in 2016 by the Islamic State is no coincidence: the governorate is home to many within Jordan’s Christian minority of roughly 300,000 people and is home to several sites featured in the Holy Bible and the Crusades.

The twin attacks have spurred the Jordanian government into action to tighten security protocols and increase the penalties for terrorist actors plotting attacks in the Kingdom. Security forces conducted overnight raids, and even airstrikes, into suspected Islamic State hideouts and hubs Jordanian intelligence agencies identified in Karak and southern Syria. On October 26-27, in response to the Karak church attack, Jordanian warplanes struck several sites in Syria’s southern Dara’a and Suwayda provinces, with the Jordanian Armed Forces reporting nearly two dozen IS militants killed and a weapons depot destroyed, though the strike caused collateral damage, with seven civilians killed. This temporarily raised tensions with the new Syrian administration. Jordanian forces also conducted several raids and checks in response to the Sri Lankan Embassy attack, with raids in Karak Governorate’s Mazar and areas around Amman such as Jubeiha and northern Marqa, Russeifa, and Al-Rajm al-Shami.

On November 8, the government introduced an updated counterterrorism strategy, with some new policies and approaches immediately in effect and others to be approved by Jordan’s Parliament in the next two weeks. These initiatives include restrictions on early release for individuals convicted of terrorism charges, the removal of the practice of shortening prison sentences on the premise of good behavior, raising the minimum sentence period from five to ten or 15 years, and surveilling former convicts after incarceration through house arrest or electronic monitoring. The government would also increase punitive measures for individuals who play a more peripheral role in terrorist acts, such as individuals who assist or incite terrorism through operational assistance or hate speech.

Broader questions remain, however, about whether these measures — largely centered around punitive measures — will effectively close the gap and prevent further plots, particularly alongside a trend of increased activity amongst IS sleeper cells in neighboring Syria and Iraq. Ten years after Jordan’s last major terrorist attack, it is clear that the network is undertaking a strategy in late 2026 to target the Kingdom and test whether the country can serve as a soft target, launching attacks against a diverse range of targets as the terrorist group recalibrates its strategy.

The post Is Jordan Back in the Crosshairs of Terrorist Groups? appeared first on The Soufan Center.

item.title: After Trump’s Midterm Setback, Middle East on Edge for What Happens Next
item.dc:creator: Nikkie Lyubarsky
item.description:
After widespread losses for President Trump’s Republican Party in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, Middle East regional leaders, particularly those embroiled in the various conflicts there, are recalibrating their decisions in light of expected policy shifts in Washington. Internal deliberations in both Iran, an adversary, and Israel, a U.S. ally, will be influenced by […]

The post After Trump’s Midterm Setback, Middle East on Edge for What Happens Next appeared first on The Soufan Center.
item.content:encoded:
After widespread losses for President Trump’s Republican Party in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, Middle East regional leaders, particularly those embroiled in the various conflicts there, are recalibrating their decisions in light of expected policy shifts in Washington. Internal deliberations in both Iran, an adversary, and Israel, a U.S. ally, will be influenced by the U.S. election, and the outcome of these debates might determine whether conflicts still raging in the region are settled or escalate.

Trump’s team, including Vice President J.D. Vance, who has been the key U.S. mediator in settlement talks with Iran, has written publicly that the Iran war as well as seemingly unconditional U.S. support for Israel’s actions were major contributors to the election outcome. Iranian officials and commentators have cheered the Democrats’ gains in the United States as further evidence of the success of Iran’s strategy to counter the U.S.-Israeli attack that began February 28. Tehran has cast the vote as a rejection of the U.S. decision to initiate the war, and the failure of the U.S.-Israeli vision that the war would easily succeed in toppling an Iranian regime weakened after a major uprising in January. After the U.S. vote, Iranian parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf said Americans had rejected war and that Tehran endorsed their message. Mohsen Reza’i, the hardline veteran Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander who, as the new Secretary-General of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), has emerged as perhaps a paramount decision-maker, stated that Iran had “inflicted a major strategic defeat on Trump on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz” and “a heavy political defeat in Washington.”

Iranian leaders remain divided, however, on whether the election results ensure that Trump will not follow through on his threat to renew attacks on Iran after the vote. He remains Commander-in-Chief and no longer faces U.S. voters before leaving office in January 2029. The incoming U.S. Congress does not take office until January, and even after its inauguration, congressional efforts to end the war through funding cuts or other legislative action face Trump’s veto power. Some Iranian leaders warn that the politically weakened Trump could become more dangerous to Iran after the election defeat. A senior Iranian political source told Amwaj media that Trump “is a wounded wild animal right now,” adding: “Our guard is not down.” Tehran has indicated it is prepared to respond to any new U.S. escalation with “zero red lines” attacks on Arab Gulf state infrastructure and U.S.-linked targets.

As Tehran remains buoyant but watchful, U.S. officials appear to read the election results as a mandate to redouble the diplomatic search for a settlement. Trump and his team reportedly perceive that mediation by Qatar and Pakistan is advancing and deserves more time to bear fruit. On Friday, Trump spoke with Qatar’s Emir Sheik Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss “Qatar’s mediation efforts toward a comprehensive agreement with Iran to end the regional crisis,” according to a Qatari statement. The statement added that the Qatari ruler stressed the importance of avoiding further escalation, ensuring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, and securing energy supplies. According to a wide range of reports, in recent weeks Trump has rebuffed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s push for a renewed attack on Iran.

Trump is maintaining existing economic and military pressure on Iran to drive Tehran toward a deal. On Friday, Trump confirmed the U.S. had carried out a “small-scale strike” on air defense sites on Iran’s Qeshm Island, which Iran uses as a key staging ground to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Additional small-scale U.S. strikes on Iranian air defenses apparently took place Saturday. Also on Saturday, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) stated it had formed a task force “to prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials” – an operation apparently intended to block Russian shipments of weaponry and technology to Iran via the Caspian Sea.

Saudi leaders are attempting to judge how the U.S. vote might affect Saudi security requirements and broader U.S.-Saudi relations. In September, Washington declined a request by de facto leader Mohammad bin Salman (MBS) for direct U.S. military help rolling back ground advances by the Houthi movement in Yemen. U.S. officials instead opted to provide more modest assistance, including expanded intelligence cooperation to help the Saudis and their Yemeni partners target Houthi units. The U.S. election presumably will reinforce Trump’s reluctance to be drawn more deeply into the ground conflict in Yemen, particularly insofar as the current, Republican-led Congress has not enacted an Authorization for the Use of Military Force (AUMF) for U.S. military operations in Yemen (or in Iran). On the other hand, the Trump team might assess that more direct U.S. intervention to defeat the Iran-backed Houthis will put pressure on Tehran – without requiring escalation against Iran itself.

MBS and his team are also concerned the U.S. election might upend the recent bilateral U.S.-Saudi civilian nuclear accord. Many in Congress, of both U.S. parties, questioned the pact for omitting a binding prohibition on the enrichment of uranium by the Kingdom – an agreement structure not consistent with past U.S. non-proliferation policy. An earlier U.S. accord with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) does not permit the Emirates to enrich uranium and therefore comported with longstanding U.S. policy. The U.S.-Saudi pact also violated the understanding of many in the U.S. Congress that the agreement would be contingent on Saudi normalization with Israel – a step MBS has repeatedly rejected until there is a clear pathway toward the establishment of an independent Palestinian state.

Perhaps nowhere in the region has the U.S. election reverberated more than in Israel, where the outcome of its own election one week prior became inextricably linked to the U.S. midterm vote. In Israel, neither the bloc led by Netanyahu nor his main opponent, former Israel Defense Forces (IDF) Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, won a majority in the 120-seat Israeli parliament. Both leaders sought to assemble the needed 61+ seat governing coalition. As Eisenkot and Netanyahu jockeyed for position, Trump’s electoral setback – which U.S. and Israeli analysts attributed to the effects of the Iran war – convinced Israeli political elites that Netanyahu’s role in starting the Iran war had jeopardized the country’s vital U.S. support.

Israeli fears were realized on Tuesday morning (Election Day), when Trump unexpectedly announced that the nearly $4 billion in annual U.S. security aid to Israel would terminate immediately – at the end of 2026. The aid termination timeframe – two years before the end of 2028 deadline previously agreed between the two governments in a Memorandum of Understanding – shocked many Israeli leaders. Israel uses the aid to finance the purchase of U.S.-made weaponry. Trump’s team expressed publicly that the immediate aid cutoff was intended to deprive critics of the argument that the Trump administration provides Israel unconditional support, ignoring its violations of international law and its abuses against Palestinians under its control.

Intensifying their efforts to forge a coalition that would oust Netanyahu, Eisenkot’s bloc softened its opposition to accepting support from the two main Arab lists, which together control 19 seats. On Saturday, Israeli President Isaac Herzog, assessing that Eisenkot had a better chance than Netanyahu to assemble a majority, gave Eisenkot a mandate to try to form a government. He has 28 days to succeed, with the potential to extend that timeframe an additional 14 days. Yet it remains unclear how an Eisenkot government, if formed, will repair the damaged U.S. public perceptions of Israel. He and his bloc’s views on regional issues are similar to those of Netanyahu, including commitment to end Hamas’ rule and dismantle its military structure in Gaza. Eisenkot and his allies also seek to end the threat posed by another core Iranian partner, Lebanese Hezbollah, including through continued IDF operations in southern Lebanon. Eisenkot’s supporters claim that his commitment to preventing and prosecuting Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in the West Bank, and to releasing tax and customs duties Netanyahu withheld from the Palestinian Authority, will start rebuilding Israel’s image in the U.S.

The post After Trump’s Midterm Setback, Middle East on Edge for What Happens Next appeared first on The Soufan Center.

item.title: Iran War Recalibrates Regional Expectations and Assumptions
item.dc:creator: Nikkie Lyubarsky
item.description:
As U.S. and Iranian officials acknowledge some progress toward a settlement, the U.S.-Iran war will require regional leaders to reassess decades of assumptions about the region’s security architecture. The post Iran War Recalibrates Regional Expectations and Assumptions appeared first on The Soufan Center.
item.content:encoded:
As U.S. and Iranian officials acknowledge some progress toward a settlement, the U.S.-Iran war will require regional leaders to reassess decades of assumptions about the region’s security architecture. The region’s approaches to security are likely to undergo wholesale change no matter the terms of any U.S.-Iran settlement, even if that solution meets U.S. demands for significant limitations on Iran’s nuclear program. Regional leaders will also need to revisit the relative weight they have attached to security concerns as compared to economic diversification initiatives.

Since President Trump, in his first term, withdrew from the 2015 multilateral Iran nuclear agreement, many regional leaders assessed that a U.S.-led war to topple the ruling regime in Tehran was a distinct possibility. That perception took hold in the region even as U.S. public opinion recoiled against the U.S. experiences in Iraq and Afghanistan, and President Trump promised not to engage in another “regime change” war against a Middle Eastern foe. Regional leaders believed Iran’s refusal to negotiate a new nuclear agreement, either with Trump or with President Biden’s administration, made a U.S. war against Iran almost inevitable. The region’s leaders hoped — though not necessarily expected — that war with the U.S. would cause the Islamic regime in Tehran to collapse or capitulate under the weight of the massive employment of U.S. airpower.

Yet Iran’s resilience in the face of an intensive U.S. and Israeli bombing campaign, coupled with its ability to control the flow of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, has shattered the regional illusion that Iran’s regime could be defeated. The results of the U.S. midterm elections illustrate the domestic political consequences of a prolonged, inconclusive war against a determined Iranian regime that sits astride a major global energy chokepoint. Iran’s ability to pelt the region with missiles and drones has placed decades of U.S. forward positioning of 40,000 U.S. forces in a string of military facilities in the Arab Gulf states and the broader region in jeopardy.

The U.S. is highly unlikely to leave the region entirely, whether the bases that were heavily damaged by Iran’s missiles and drones are abandoned or rebuilt. But the deterrent effect of the U.S. forward positioning has been lost. And the U.S. war effort has convinced regional leaders that, in all likelihood, neither President Trump nor any future president will authorize the major ground invasion that would be required to remove the regime — absent the conduct of an Iranian mass casualty terrorist attack on the U.S. or its interests, an all-out Iranian sprint toward a nuclear weapon, or a strike that sinks a U.S. capital warship.

Regional leaders have resigned themselves to the fact that they will be challenged by a regime in Tehran that has no expiration date. Even though the regime assesses the U.S. as an existential threat, its leadership and/or security apparatus, led by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), are not likely to undertake an operation that risks provoking a large-scale U.S. reaction. And without outside intervention, there is little hope that another major domestic uprising, similar to that which was crushed in January, will topple the regime.

Some in the region fear that Iran’s regime might retreat into a North Korea-like, highly militarized insularity. Under this model, Iranian leaders could be expected to redouble their focus on developing advanced missiles and drones, and potentially also building up Iran’s ground forces capability to guard against potential invasion. Global experts perceive the regime’s takeaway from the war is that North Korea’s approach is the one model that can assure Iran’s security – that only a nuclear-armed state is immune from the U.S. or other attacks. And some argue Iran is already proceeding down this pathway: Iranian hardline figures have begun openly advocating for abrogating or overriding the late Supreme Leader Ali Khamene’i’s religious directive (fatwa) prohibiting the development of an Iranian nuclear weapon. And that debate is said to be broadening to mainstream discussion among Iran’s elites. Unlike North Korea, Iran is currently assessed as lacking a credible capacity to invade its neighbors. But there are concerns that Iran might seek to develop a more significant offensive conventional military capability by augmenting its ground forces and amphibious landing capacity.

Beyond rebuilding and augmenting its central capabilities, the regime in Tehran is likely to double down on its long-established “forward defense” effort centered on arming and funding regional non-state actors. Two of its allies, Hamas and Lebanese Hezbollah, have been severely weakened over the past three years by Israeli operations. Another, a constellation of Iran-backed militias in Iraq, is under pressure from the Baghdad government, which seeks reintegration into the Arab fold. Iran’s other close ally, the Houthi movement in Yemen, is embroiled in a conflict with Saudi Arabia, in the process using Iran-supplied missiles and drones against civilian targets in the Kingdom. But aggressive attacks on U.S., European, or Middle East targets by Iran’s allies risk causing the very mass-casualty event that might shift U.S. and European opinion toward all-out conflict with Tehran.

In pursuit of absolute security, Iran’s leaders will also work to shore up their strategic relationships with Russia and China. Iran looks to both powers for a steady supply of vital military technology and help circumventing Washington’s interlocking web of sanctions. Most of the sanctions are likely to remain even if the U.S. and Iran settle the conflict. As has North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, Iran is likely to play off Moscow and Beijing against each other to maximize the support it receives. However, Tehran will not find unconditional support from China, which, unlike Russia, is a major oil and gas buyer and wants stability in the Persian Gulf. On Monday, President Xi Jinping hosted in Beijing Iran’s closest Gulf partner, Sultan Haythim bin Tariq Al Said of Oman, as well as senior officials from Iran and Saudi Arabia, for talks aimed at de-escalation in the Gulf. Also on Monday, China’s Foreign Ministry announced that its senior officials would visit seven countries in the Persian Gulf and the Horn of Africa to promote regional de-escalation.

A major question is how the region would respond to an Iran working intently to develop a nuclear weapon. A nuclear-armed Iran would present the U.S. and its allies with a worst-case scenario — a “perfect storm” — in the form of a regional nuclear arms race that U.S. policymakers have sought to head off for at least four decades. The de facto leader of Saudi Arabia, Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman (MBS), restated in a Fox News interview in 2023 that: “We are concerned of any country getting a nuclear weapon,” and if Iran acquires a nuclear weapon, “we will have to get one.” A recent U.S.-Saudi civilian nuclear “123 Agreement,” long under discussion between the two governments, would alter prior U.S. non-proliferation policy by permitting the Saudis to enrich uranium domestically. Saudi Arabia also has close relations with another regional nuclear state, Pakistan. The U.S.-Saudi nuclear agreement contrasts with an earlier U.S.-UAE “123 Agreement,” which prohibited domestic uranium enrichment and reprocessing. Although that pact would not provide the UAE the capability, technically, to develop a nuclear weapon, Abu Dhabi has forged close strategic relations with Israel, which is widely understood to possess a significant nuclear arsenal. Other regional powers, including Türkiye and Egypt, are said to be likely to consider developing a nuclear weapons capability if Iran does.

The war has also presented regional leaders with the realization that they will need to spend more on their own defense — to harden energy sites, add to their missile and drone defenses, and perform other upgrades. The Gulf leaders will also better position their ground forces to counter Iran and its allies, such as the Houthis. Many experts assess the regional states will continue to look to mutual defense pacts and other regional security solutions, even as they remain strategically engaged with the United States. The newly-forged Mecca Joint Defense Agreement committing Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan to each other’s defense has proved of limited utility to Saudi Arabia in its ground battle against the Houthi forces in Yemen. Egypt and perhaps Syria are widely tipped to join that pact, giving it additional strategic weight. Even if additional moderate Arab leaders or other regional countries join that or other groupings, these alliances would not compensate for a U.S. retreat from the region. A cogent analysis of the balance of forces explains why no regional leader has yet suggested abandoning strategic relations with the United States in favor of regional solutions.

The post Iran War Recalibrates Regional Expectations and Assumptions appeared first on The Soufan Center.
